exercises.text: Suppose the range for 5.0MeVα ray is known to be 2.0 mm in a certain material. Does this mean that every 5.0MeVα a ray that strikes this material travels 2.0 mm, or does the range have an average value with some statistical fluctuations in the distances traveled? Explain.
exercises.reason: Add the missing foundational identification task; retain the statistical-range idea without awkward duplicate “a ray” wording.
exercises.proposed: (a) Identify the particles emitted as alpha radiation, beta-minus radiation, beta-plus radiation, and gamma radiation. (b) An alpha particle of a given energy has a quoted range of 2.0 mm in a material. Does every such particle stop at exactly 2.0 mm? Explain.

exercises.text: What is the difference between γ rays and characteristic X-rays? Is either necessarily more energetic than the other? Which can be the most energetic?
exercises.reason: Useful connection to the earlier X-ray/quantum material; distinguish photon origin from energy alone.

exercises.text: Ionizing radiation interacts with matter by scattering from electrons and nuclei in the substance. Based on the law of conservation of momentum and energy, explain why electrons tend to absorb more energy than nuclei in these interactions.

exercises.text: What characteristics of radioactivity show it to be nuclear in origin and not atomic?

exercises.text: What is the source of the energy emitted in radioactive decay? Identify an earlier conservation law, and describe how it was modified to take such processes into account.
exercises.reason: Use total energy and rest mass directly, without suggesting that energy conservation failed.
exercises.proposed: Where does the energy released in radioactive decay come from? Explain how the total rest mass of the products can be smaller than that of the parent while total energy is conserved.

exercises.text: Consider . If an electric field is substituted for the magnetic field with positive charge instead of the north pole and negative charge instead of the south pole, in which directions will the α, β , and γ rays bend?

exercises.proposed: Alpha particles, beta-minus particles, beta-plus particles, and gamma rays travel horizontally between two plates. The upper plate is positive and the lower plate is negative. exercises.text: Arrange the following according to their ability to act as radiation shields, with the best first and worst last. Explain your ordering in terms of how radiation loses its energy in matter.(a) A solid material with low density composed of low-mass atoms. (b) A gas composed of high-mass atoms. (c) A gas composed of low-mass atoms. (d) A solid with high density composed of high-mass atoms.
exercises.reason: Replace an under-specified ranking across gases/solids with representative shielding and attenuation reasoning.
exercises.proposed: For typical radioactive-source energies, explain why paper can stop alpha particles, a suitable thickness of plastic can stop beta particles, and much thicker shielding is usually needed to substantially reduce gamma radiation. Why does “reducing the gamma intensity” describe shielding more accurately than “stopping every gamma photon”?

exercises.text: Often, when people have to work around radioactive materials spills, we see them wearing white coveralls (usually a plastic material). What types of radiation (if any) do you think these suits protect the worker from, and how?
exercises.reason: Distinguish contamination control from shielding of penetrating radiation.
exercises.proposed: Workers handling radioactive contamination may wear disposable coveralls and gloves. Explain what these prevent. Why do such garments provide little shielding against penetrating gamma rays?

exercises.text: Is it possible for light emitted by a scintillator to be too low in frequency to be used in a photomultiplier tube? Explain.

exercises.text: The energy of 30.0 eV is required to ionize a molecule of the gas inside a Geiger tube, thereby producing an ion pair. Suppose a particle of ionizing radiation deposits 0.500 MeV of energy in this Geiger tube. What maximum number of ion pairs can it create?

exercises.text: A particle of ionizing radiation creates 4000 ion pairs in the gas inside a Geiger tube as it passes through. What minimum energy was deposited, if 30.0 eV is required to create each ion pair?
